result.text:
# Talk about making love before you do it
From here on, when I say making love, I'm talking about two people who care about each other deeply and feel super connected, using their bodies as part of that connection. If you’ve never experienced this, it may be like trying to explain the taste of an orange. If you don’t know what love is, you don’t know. That’s another conversation, and I'd suggest reading my inner child reparenting guide.
Having sex is just the physical act, whether that connection is there or not. But sometimes it can create the connection also.
That last part matters because the act may change the connection. But most couples wait until they’re already having sex before they talk honestly about it. By then a truthful answer might interrupt something that has begun. Earlier, the conversation can still go places the later one often can’t. Having it is already part of the difference between making love together and merely having sex.
Some things you may know now. What does sex mean to you—recreation, bonding, sacred practice, stress relief, all of those, or something else? What do you actually desire? What helps your body feel safe? Are there kinks or particular dynamics that matter? What has your history taught you about your erotic wiring? What reliably doesn't work? How often do you each imagine wanting sex?
Some answers you may not know yet. A lot of people can’t answer cleanly because they don’t know. That’s still an answer. *I don’t know, but I’m willing to find out honestly with you* is a much better beginning than silently assuming the bodies will somehow negotiate everything on their own.
The way two people handle that uncertainty tells me something already. Sexual compatibility isn’t just whether two bodies fit. It’s whether two people can stay honest while maximally exposed. If you can talk frankly before your clothes come off, you’ve practiced some of the trust, attention, and willingness to be seen that making love requires.
The frequency question can come back differently with time. In a long relationship, one person usually wants more sex, less sex, or different sex for at least some stretch. What would that mismatch mean, and how might you handle it? It’s one of the great factories of quiet resentment. Talking before either person is hurt won’t solve it in advance, but it gives you somewhere to begin.
